rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3.1-3.4 report the authors' own model runs (monthly soil water balance IR = ETc - EP computed on WorldClim pixels over the PPA), validation against 73 weather stations (Figure 3), water deficit maps (Figure 5, Table 2) and an ANN relevance analysis of ITCZ influence (Figure 6).
rows.notes: The study computes and maps the monthly irrigation requirement of Hass avocado across Colombia's potential production area using a simplified soil water balance (not an energy balance model) fed with WorldClim 1970-2000 averages; it finds 99.8% of the area needs irrigation at least one month a year. It does not implement or evaluate any scheduling tool/app on farms, does not measure irrigation applications, water savings, or water use at phenological stages. At most it supports a precondition (identifying when/where water deficit occurs) for scheduling; the claimed effect of reducing unnecessary applications is not tested. The modelling approach (water balance from gridded climate data) also differs from the 'energy balance models' named in the passage.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3.1-3.4 report the authors' own model computations (monthly IR maps over the PPA), validation with weather station data (Figure 3) and ANN relevance analysis (Figure 6).
rows.notes: No yield or productivity data are reported by this study. The only productivity statement (yield increase with drip irrigation, Section 4.2) is cited from Grajales [23], not the authors' own result. The study only maps water deficit months/periods (Figures 4-6, Table 2) as a precondition for irrigation scheduling; it does not test whether scheduling maintains productivity, and the model is a soil water balance rather than an energy balance model.

notes: Full text appears complete (pages 1-17 including references). The study is a regional GIS/climate-data modelling exercise producing irrigation requirement maps; it contains no field trial of irrigation scheduling, no measured water applications, and no yield measurements, so it cannot support claims about app/model-based scheduling reducing water use or maintaining productivity.
